title: Bizarre vending machine in Melbourne full of anti-overdose medication
text:
By ASHLEY NICKEL, NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  23:24 AEST, 8 September 2026   |  Updated:  23:30 AEST, 8 September 2026

37

View  comments

The location of a new anti-overdose vending machine has ignited debate over whether its installation will save lives or worsen an opioid crisis.

Locals in and around Victoria Street in North Richmond, 3km west of Melbourne CBD, have been 'terrorised' by a growing number of ice and heroin users.

The Victorian Government in June announced it would trial a naloxone vending machine on the street as part of a $95million plan to reduce drug-related deaths and injury.

Naloxone is a fast-acting drug that temporarily reverses opioid overdose from heroin, fentanyl and prescription painkillers.

The vending machines will also be trialled in Brimbank, Sunshine, Darebin and regional centres Shepparton, Ballarat and Mildura.

Yarra Mayor Stephen Jolly wrote a letter to Health Minister Ingrid Stitt to oppose the Victoria Street machine.

He said his council 'has concerns about the cumulative impact if the machine is installed in the vicinity of Victoria Street in Richmond'.

'As you are aware, the location of the Medically Supervised Injecting Room at the Richmond housing estate has had an impact on safety in the area, impacting local traders and the community,' the letter, seen by News.com.au, read.

A proposal to install a naloxone vending machine (like above) on Victoria Street in North Richmond has ignited debate

'While Council is working to address this and revitalise the area, we are concerned that a Naloxone dispensing machine will compound the issues facing the area.'

Drug users injecting in full public view has already become a common sight on Victoria Street, which is just a few hundred metres from the state's only supervised injecting room on Lennox Street.

The room allows users to inject drugs with clean equipment and with medical assistance at hand.

However, a loophole banning police from making drug arrests near the room has led to a spike in public use and crime.

The room's location is especially controversial as it is next door to a primary school.

Mr Jolly said the proposed naloxone machine would be a 'kick in the teeth' to local residents and business owners already struggling with increased crime due to the injection room.

He cited already high tensions about the room and urged the government to choose another location for the vending machine.

'We told them we support these dispensing units because they save lives, but because it was such a toxic and fraught situation in that area of North Richmond, where everyone's already under siege, it needs to be done with community input,' Mr Jolly said.

Response to the machine (above) was torn between the need to reduce drug-related harm and the grim reality of higher crime for locals

'We had doubts about putting it on Victoria Street because it's just going to p**s off all the traders and cause an unnecessary drama. It was just poking the bear.'

However, Greens MP Gabrielle de Vietri slammed Mr Jolly's opposition for putting users 'at a higher risk of dying'.

'You do not make our community safer by making an overdose antidote harder to reach,' she said.

'This is NIMBY-ism at its most dangerous. Harm-reduction decisions should be based on evidence not political pressure. The mayor should be fighting stigma, not feeding it.'

Mr Jolly shot back, telling Ms Vietri 'don't call us NIMBYs mate' while highlighting that most people in Richmond remained sympathetic to drug-related harm while living with the effects of the injecting room.

'It's also not ideal to have drug users roam around the streets after they've shot up,' he said.

'...There needs to be more supervised injecting facilities so we're not carrying the load for the whole city.

'We're named NIMBYs. It's ridiculous. We're not saying close our supervised injecting room. But imagine if you had one pub in Melbourne and it was next to your house.'

Yarra Mayor Stephen Jolly said that while the vending machines (like above) were a good idea, it wasn't fair for Richmond to 'carrying the load' of drug harm reduction 'for the whole city'

The response online was similarly mixed with some pushing for more drug-related harm reduction while others highlighted the toll on the local community.

'This is an unhinged take. I'd love anyone who is against naloxone being provided for free to the community to explain to me how they think it works,' one person wrote.

'The fact is, naloxone saves lives, has no effect on people other than reversing the effects of opiates.

'No drug user is seeking naloxone for kicks but if someone finds themselves in trouble it is literally a matter of life and death.'

Another said: 'North Richmond already has an open drug market, assaults, knife violence, arson and anti-social behaviour and the problem is a machine that can stop someone dying from an overdose?'
